title: Uni-DHC: Adaptive Hypergraph Clustering Beyond Homophily
one_liner: Instead of assuming neighboring nodes are alike, learn to treat each relationship type differently based on the data.
lead: Most graph clustering methods assume that if two nodes are connected, they are similar — a feature called homophily. But real-world networks often break this rule: in a social network, someone might connect to people unlike them; in a knowledge graph, related concepts can be different. This paper proposes Uni-DHC, which learns to weight different connection types differently instead of using a fixed rule.

paras: When you cluster nodes in a graph, you want nodes that belong together to sit near each other. The oldest trick is homophily: if two nodes connect, assume they are in the same cluster. This works when the network is 'clean' — a friendship network where friends really do like each other.

But it fails when connections mean something else. In a citation network, a paper might cite a foundational work it strongly disagrees with. In a knowledge graph, 'opposite' and 'similar' are both real relationships. When adjacent nodes are actually from different clusters, fixed propagation methods (which treat all connections the same way) spread wrong information and mess up the clustering.

callout.b: Fixed propagation treats every connection the same, so heterophilic data (where neighbors are unlike) breaks the clustering.
callout.html: Learn to weight each relationship type differently based on what the data shows.

steps.text: Instead of just pairs of nodes, look at groups of 3, 4, or more nodes connected together (a hyperedge).

steps.b: Learn a weight for each order
steps.text: Assign a learnable number to pairs, triples, quadruples, etc., based on how useful each is for clustering.
Blend the signals from each order type, where weights determine how much to trust each.
Ensure that different hyperedges do not all send the same message (decorrelation); ensure each node does not simply copy its neighbors (node-level consistency).
The result is a set of node groupings that cluster correctly even when neighbors are different.

paras: Uni-DHC replaces the fixed propagation formula with a learnable function. In standard methods, every connection contributes the same; here, each connection type (pairs, triples, or larger groups) has its own learned importance score that adapts to the data.

hidden.name: multi-order importance scores
paras: The method learns a separate importance score for each level of grouping: how important are pairs of connected nodes, versus triples, versus larger groups. These scores are hidden but measurable — they tell us whether the data prefers simple pairwise links or complex group relationships.

The paper estimates these by minimizing a loss function that rewards correct clustering and penalizes redundant or contradictory messages from different hyperedges. Higher scores mean that order contributes more to the final node embeddings (learned representations).

heat.caption: Darker means higher learned importance. Pairs dominate in some datasets, triples in others.

reads.html: You are trying to guess which people in a room are friends. You could use direct friendships (pairs). But you could also look at groups who do things together (triples). In a real social network, maybe pairs matter more than triples for clustering; in another dataset, the opposite is true. Uni-DHC learns which one matters by looking at the data.

The method learns a set of weights, one per hypergraph order, that mix high-order neighborhood information. From a spectral perspective, this creates a learnable polynomial filter (instead of a fixed low-pass filter), allowing the method to adjust its 'frequency response' to the data.

mechanism.h2: Why learning multi-order weights fixes heterophily
paras: In a homophilic network, all relationship types point the same direction: if A and B are neighbors, they are the same. A fixed weight works fine. But in heterophilic data, some relationships mean 'same' and others mean 'different'. A fixed method cannot distinguish them.

Uni-DHC assigns a learned number to each relationship type. When training on real data with correct labels, the method learns: 'type-A links are usually within-cluster, so use a high number for them; type-B links often cross clusters, so use a low or negative number.' This adaptive numbering stops wrong signals from drowning out the right ones, because now high-quality signals get amplified and bad signals get dampened.

Additionally, the paper adds two constraints: a node-level consistency term (saying each node's learned representation should be close to the average of its neighbors, to make training stable) and a hyperedge-level decorrelation term (saying different hyperedges should not all send the same information, to prevent all hyperedges from cancelling each other out). Together, these prevent the method from getting stuck in bad solutions.

stages.s: Raw hypergraph: nodes and multi-order connections
Learn importance score for each order type
Mix neighborhood signals, weighted by learned scores

math.words: Total loss is: node embedding quality, plus node consistency penalty, plus hyperedge decorrelation penalty.
math.equation: L = L_cluster + lambda_node * L_consistency + lambda_edge * L_decorr
symbols: loss from clustering objective (e.g., minimize within-cluster distance)
penalty if a node's embedding is far from its neighbors' average
penalty if different hyperedges send redundant information
weight controlling how strongly to enforce node consistency
weight controlling how strongly to enforce edge decorrelation

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a dataset has 4 nodes split into 2 true clusters: {A, B} and {C, D}.
Initial guess: all relationship types matter equally (all weights = 0.5).
Training data shows: A-B and C-D are pairwise neighbors, but A-C and B-D are both in the same hyperedge.
Uni-DHC learns: pairwise weight = 0.8 (encourages same-cluster clustering), hyperedge weight = -0.2 (penalizes within-hyperedge mixing because this hyperedge bridges clusters).
Result: when propagating, pairwise signals dominate, and A and B end up similar to each other, as does C and D. Clusters emerge correctly even though the hyperedge structure was 'wrong'.

math.note: The learnable weights adapt the filter's response to the data, letting it pass the right signals (within-cluster links) and suppress the wrong ones (cross-cluster links).

charts.note: Fixed weighting works on homophilic data but fails badly when neighbors are unlike.

charts.title: Uni-DHC (learnable weights)
charts.note: Learning each order's importance keeps clustering strong even when adjacency is unreliable.

items.html: If the method learns scores for pairs, triples, quadruples, and higher, the model can overfit, learning that a specific order is important in the training set but not in new data. The decorrelation constraint helps by forcing different hyperedges to stay distinct, so they do not all converge on the same false pattern. But on very large datasets, you may need to add extra penalties to prevent any one order from dominating unfairly.

Enforcing consistency (nodes stay close to neighbor average) while also decorrelating hyperedges can create tension during training. If lambda values are badly tuned, the method may not converge cleanly.

items.b: Heterophily must be measurable in hyperedges.
items.html: If the dataset is heterophilic but all high-order hyperedges are also heterophilic (so no order type is reliable), the method cannot recover. It needs at least some orders that correlate with true clusters.

Set lambda values based on data size and hypergraph density. Test learned weights on a validation set to confirm they are interpretable. Use the method when you have reason to believe heterophily plays a role.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small synthetic hypergraph with known clusters and a mix of homophilic and heterophilic edges. Train Uni-DHC and a baseline fixed-propagation method. Visualize: (1) the learned importance scores for each order type, (2) the final node embeddings in 2D (via dimensionality reduction), and (3) the cluster assignments.
demo.metric_eq: clustering_accuracy = (number of correctly clustered nodes) / (total nodes)
demo.closing: The demo should show that Uni-DHC learns different weights for each order type (not all the same), and that it clusters more correctly than fixed propagation, especially when the graph is heterophilic — because the learned weights let it amplify signals from reliable relationship types and suppress signals from unreliable ones.
